strengths: The paper is technically sound and the empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: 17 diverse real-world regression datasets, 10 random splits, five metrics (PICP, NIW, NCIW, quantile loss, interval score), three CLEAR variants with different base-model pools, and ablations corresponding exactly to the fixed baselines (λ=1, γ1=1), plus additional baselines (Naive, UACQR-S/P) in the appendix.

The residual-based quantile regression for aleatoric uncertainty (fitting quantiles on residuals Yi − f̂(Xi) rather than directly on targets) is a simple, well-motivated idea that demonstrably improves stability of the aleatoric component (ALEATORIC vs. ALEATORIC-R comparisons).

The dual-parameter calibration scheme (γ1 for scale, λ for the epistemic/aleatoric ratio) is conceptually clean, and the case study on Ames Housing nicely illustrates that the learned λ adapts sensibly across information regimes (λ=0.6 with 2 features vs. λ=14.5 with all features).

The paper is honest about its guarantees: it acknowledges that the default implementation reuses the validation set as calibration set (breaking strict conformal guarantees) and provides a 'Conformalized CLEAR' variant in Appendix G with a finite-sample marginal coverage proof, plus a discussion of asymptotic conditional coverage (Lemma 2.1).

The related-work treatment (Appendix A) is extensive and fair, positioning the contribution precisely against UACQR, deep ensembles, MC dropout, GPRs, BNNs, EPISCORE, and TabPFN, and even quantifying where the gap to UACQR narrows when all methods share the same base modules.

Simulations targeting conditional coverage as a function of distance from the training data (sphere-radius test point generation) directly probe the extrapolation behavior that the method claims to fix.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is modest: CLEAR essentially scales two pre-estimated interval-width components (ensemble-based epistemic, quantile-regression-based aleatoric) with two hyperparameters tuned on validation data. The closest prior work (UACQR) already tunes the ratio; the main deltas are (i) additionally tuning γ1 and (ii) fitting aleatoric quantiles on residuals. The authors themselves concede that when all methods use identical base modules, the gap over UACQR narrows substantially.

Tuning λ over a grid of ~4000 values on a validation set that is also the calibration set raises both overfitting and miscalibration concerns. The empirical PICP staying at 0.95 is reassuring but is an empirical observation, not a guarantee for the default procedure; no selection-aware correction or study of sensitivity to calibration-set size is provided.

The headline improvements over the strongest baseline are small: CLEAR improves NCIW by only ~3% over ALEATORIC-R (which is itself the authors' improved CQR variant), so much of the reported 17.4%/28.2% gains come from comparisons against weaker baselines or the authors' own intermediate constructions. A comparison against a fixed, non-PCS, standard CQR implementation with deep ensembles as the epistemic component would strengthen the generality claim.

Claims about improved conditional coverage are supported only in simulations; on the real-world datasets only marginal coverage and average width/loss metrics are reported, so the central 'better conditional coverage' narrative is not directly validated on real data (e.g., no subgroup- or distance-binned coverage analysis).

Lemma 2.1 is a fairly trivial asymptotic statement requiring strong consistency of both estimators and (implicitly) i.i.d. data; it provides little insight beyond 'if everything is consistent, the method works asymptotically,' and its uniform convergence argument over Λ is only sketched.

The method inherits the computational cost of the PCS framework (100+ bootstrap refits, model selection over N1×N2 pipelines), and the paper does not quantify runtime or provide a wall-clock comparison against cheaper alternatives like deep ensembles with post-hoc calibration, despite acknowledging scalability limitations.

Several presentation issues: the theoretical contribution is scattered between the main text and appendices, the notation distinguishes ˆq_epi vs q̂^epi inconsistently, and some claims (e.g., 'the first to introduce two calibration parameters') feel overstated given prior work on ratio-tuned combinations.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 17 real-world datasets, 10 random splits per dataset, three model variants (a/b/c), multiple ablations (fixed λ=1, fixed γ1=1, Naive, UACQR), and full metric tables in the appendix; the experiments are detailed and reproducible in spirit, with hyperparameters and base models documented.

The residual-based aleatoric estimator (quantile regression on residuals Y_i - f_hat(X_i) rather than on Y directly) is a sensible and empirically supported contribution; it stabilizes the aleatoric component and appears to drive much of the improvement.

Honest limitations section; the appendix provides a modified 'Conformalized CLEAR' procedure with a finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee (Lemma G.2), and the related-work appendix (A) is unusually thorough, with a fair head-to-head discussion and comparison against UACQR.
The benchmark itself (extending PCS-UQ to quantile-regression-based methods) is a useful community resource, and the paper is clearly written overall.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is scaling two existing uncertainty estimates (CQR-style aleatoric and PCS-ensemble epistemic) with two hyperparameters, one set by standard split-conformal calibration and the other by grid search (≈4000 values) minimizing quantile loss on a held-out set. This is essentially a two-parameter calibration/tuning heuristic rather than a new statistical principle; the closest prior work (UACQR, Rossellini et al.) differs mainly by fixing γ1=1, which the authors themselves acknowledge.

The headline improvements are inflated by comparison against weaker baselines. The abstract emphasizes 28.2%/17.4% width gains, but these are against ALEATORIC and PCS; against the strongest baseline, ALEATORIC-R (which uses the authors' own residual trick), the NCIW improvement is only ~3% and quantile loss ~9.4%, with several datasets showing near-identical performance. Much of the benefit comes from the residual-based aleatoric model (contribution 2), not the two-parameter calibration (contribution 1), yet the paper leads with the latter.

The central claim that adaptively selecting λ is necessary is weakly supported by the authors' own tables: fixed-parameter variants (λ=1 or γ1=1) frequently match or achieve the best NCIW/quantile loss on many datasets (often the bolded 'best' values in Tables 7, 9, 12, 14 go to the fixed variants). No statistical significance testing is reported, only ±1 std across seeds.

The main practical procedure violates the theoretical guarantees it motivates from: D_cal = D_val is reused simultaneously for model selection (top-k base model), λ selection, and γ1 calibration, so the finite-sample conformal guarantee does not apply; the guaranteed variant (Conformalized CLEAR, Lemma G.2) is relegated to the appendix and is not the version evaluated in the experiments. The λ selection on the same validation/calibration set invites overfitting, which the authors note but do not quantify.

The theory is thin: Lemma 2.1 is essentially a direct consequence of estimator consistency (intervals converge to true conditional quantiles), and the asymptotic conditional coverage claim provides little practical insight; a single calibrated scalar λ (global) cannot deliver conditional coverage, and the pointwise 'dominance' interpretation of λ* (Sec 2.4) is heuristic rather than justified.

Some experimental hygiene issues: mixing expectiles with quantiles (Expectile GAM) is acknowledged as theoretically inconsistent yet included in model selection; one run was lost to a library bug (9 instead of 10 seeds for one dataset/variant); and the massive λ grid combined with small validation sets raises selection-bias concerns that are discussed only qualitatively.

Significance and impact are modest: the paper targets regression interval construction for tabular data with tree/boosting base models; the method is an ensemble of known components (CQR + bootstrapped ensembles + conformal calibration) and its applicability to distribution shift, classification, or large-scale/deep settings is deferred to future work.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—combining aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in conformal prediction intervals—and the proposed solution (two calibrated parameters γ1 and λ) is simple, general, and easy to implement on top of existing aleatoric/epistemic estimators.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: 17 diverse real-world datasets, 10 random splits, three model variants (a, b, c) with ablations over base models, multiple metrics (PICP, NIW, NCIW, quantile loss, interval score loss), and full per-dataset results in the appendix.

The comparisons are fair and largely self-controlled: baselines (ALEATORIC, ALEATORIC-R, PCS) share the same point predictor and uncertainty modules as CLEAR, isolating the contribution of the dual-parameter calibration; comparisons against the closest prior work UACQR are included in the appendix.

The residual-based aleatoric estimator (ALEATORIC-R, fitting quantiles on residuals rather than targets) is a sensible and empirically supported contribution, with a clear argument for its robustness (extreme underfitting degenerates gracefully to homoscedastic noise).

The paper is honest about its limitations: the reuse of Dcal = Dval violating finite-sample guarantees, sensitivity of λ to validation set size, computational overhead of ensembling, and the additivity assumption are all explicitly acknowledged. A 'Conformalized CLEAR' variant with a formal finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee is provided in Appendix G.

The related work discussion (Appendix A) is extensive and positions the contribution well against Bayesian methods, deep ensembles, UACQR, and EPISCORE, and the interpretability of λ as a diagnostic of uncertainty dominance (case study) adds practical value.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: CLEAR essentially adds a second scalar (λ) tuned by grid search on the validation set to a standard split-conformal rescaling. The closest method, UACQR [19], already tunes a similar ratio; the main delta is jointly optimizing both parameters and fitting aleatoric quantiles on residuals. This is an incremental contribution over existing work.

The theoretical contribution is thin: Lemma 2.1 is a fairly standard asymptotic consistency argument under strong assumptions (consistency of k base models and quantile estimators), and the marginal coverage result in Appendix G is a direct application of standard split conformal theory. The practically-used implementation (Dcal = Dval, both parameters optimized on the same data) lacks finite-sample guarantees, and the empirical defense rests on simulation evidence only.

The headline improvements are driven largely by weaker baselines: versus the strongest baseline (ALEATORIC-R), the NCIW gain is only ~3% (variant a), which is within plausible seed-to-seed variability for many datasets; no formal statistical significance tests are reported to support the claims of superiority.

Conditional coverage improvements are demonstrated mainly on synthetic simulations where the epistemic estimator inherently widens intervals in extrapolation regions; there is no empirical conditional-coverage evaluation on the real-world datasets, so the central 'improved conditional coverage' claim is only partially supported.

The λ selection procedure requires a grid of ~4000 values evaluated on the validation set, raising overfitting and computational concerns for small datasets that the authors acknowledge but do not quantify; no analysis of how performance degrades with validation set size is provided.

The method's dependency on the PCS framework (100+ bootstrap refits, model selection across model families) makes the reported gains hard to attribute cleanly: some of the improvement may come from the ensembling/model-selection machinery rather than the dual-parameter calibration itself, although variant (b) partially mitigates this.

Some claims of 'first to introduce' / 'we are the first' are overstated given prior work on uncertainty-aware CQR and decomposition in conformal prediction; a more nuanced positioning would be appropriate.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-executed empirical evaluation: 17 real-world regression datasets with 10 seeds, simulations (homoskedastic, heteroskedastic, multivariate extrapolation), ablation variants (a/b/c), a separate deep-learning configuration (Deep Ensembles + SQR), conformalized settings, runtime analysis, and a case study — this level of breadth exceeds typical UQ benchmarks.

Careful and honest treatment of theory: asymptotic conditional coverage (Lemma 2.1) is stated with explicit assumptions, a conformalized variant with finite-sample marginal coverage is provided (Lemma B.2), and the appendix candidly discusses limitations of conformal guarantees under exchangeability violations and the non-identifiability of conditional coverage in finite samples.

Honest framing of novelty relative to the closest competitor (UACQR): the paper explicitly analyzes the conceptual delta of optimizing both γ1 and λ versus fixing γ1=1, and includes head-to-head comparisons in the appendix, including acknowledging that the gap narrows when all base modules are held fixed.

The method is modular and shown to generalize across very different base estimators (tree-based PCS/QR and neural DE/SQR), which supports the claim that the calibration scheme — not the specific components — drives the improvement.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter tables, runtime tables, dataset statistics, and a description of model-selection frequencies across seeds.
weaknesses: Modest core novelty: the interval form is a simple additive combination of two uncertainty estimates with a grid-searched scalar ratio (λ) and conformal scaling (γ1). Relative to UACQR [19] (which tunes λ with γ1=1), the contribution is essentially one additional calibration scalar plus fitting quantile regression on residuals — engineering refinements more than a new methodological idea. The claimed 'first to introduce two calibration parameters' overstates the delta.

Headline gains are largely against the paper's own components: in variant (a), the improvement over the strongest baseline (ALEATORIC-R, which uses the same residual idea) is only ~3% NCIW and ~9.4% quantile loss; the large 28.2%/17.4% figures come from comparisons against weaker ingredients the authors themselves constructed. The main-paper comparison set contains no fully independent established competitor (CQR/UACQR comparisons are relegated to the appendix).

The central claim of improved conditional coverage is only demonstrated in simulations; real-world evaluations use marginal metrics (PICP, NIW, NCIW, quantile loss) with no conditional-coverage analysis on real data, so the practical significance of the conditional-coverage motivation is under-evidenced.

The theoretical results are close to trivial: if both uncertainty estimators are consistent and Λ is compact, calibration converging to the true quantiles is a straightforward consequence; the asymptotic guarantee does not distinguish CLEAR from simpler alternatives.

Potential overfitting of two tuned parameters on limited validation data is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed (e.g., sensitivity of results to validation-set size, or variance of λ* across seeds is only shown for variant (c)).

Presentation issues: a duplicated paragraph in Section 4.2, several typos ('archives' for 'achieves', 'distrbutional', 'exchangability', author-name errors in references), and heavy reliance on a not-yet-peer-reviewed base framework (PCS-UQ, arXiv 2025), making external validation of the components difficult.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 17 real-world regression datasets, 100+ synthetic simulations, 10 random seeds, multiple ablation variants (a/b/c), and additional experiments with Deep Ensembles and SQR, giving a broad picture of performance.

The paper is transparent about the limitations of its own guarantees: it acknowledges that the default implementation reuses the validation set for calibration, and provides a Conformalized CLEAR variant with a finite-sample marginal coverage proof (Lemma B.2) and an asymptotic conditional coverage result (Lemma 2.1).
Thoughtful discussion of metrics: the analysis of why pinball/quantile loss incentivizes truthful intervals (Appendix B.3, Examples B.3–B.6) is careful and adds value beyond the empirical results.
The method is modular and cheap: it can be applied post-hoc to existing estimators (PCS, CQR, DE, SQR), and the runtime analysis shows calibration overhead is negligible.
A thorough related-work appendix that carefully maps prior methods onto the (γ1, λ) parameterization and explains when they correspond to fixing γ1 = 1 or λ = 1.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core contribution is an additive, linearly scaled combination of two existing uncertainty estimates with two hyperparameters (γ1 and λ) tuned on a validation set. Framing prior work as 'fixing γ1 = 1 or λ = 1' makes the contribution essentially a hyperparameter search over a two-parameter family rather than a new modeling principle. Claims of being 'the first' to introduce two calibration parameters overstate the significance of this.

The two-parameter calibration creates an evaluation asymmetry: CLEAR optimizes λ over a ~4000-point grid and γ1 on the validation set, while most baselines (PCS, CQR, ALEATORIC) are calibrated with a single parameter. Some of the reported 15–28% gains may reflect this extra tuning capacity rather than genuinely better uncertainty structure; the paper acknowledges overfitting risk for small calibration sets but does not quantify how much of the gain comes from the extra parameter.

Metric design has a circular element: NCIW uses a calibration constant c_test-cal selected via an argmin condition computed against the test set, which partially undermines NCIW as an independent evaluation metric even if c ≈ 1 in practice. Model selection and λ tuning also use the same validation set (D_cal = D_val), so the primary comparison metric (quantile loss) partially shares data with the tuning procedure.

Theoretical guarantees are weak relative to the empirical claims: Lemma 2.1 is only asymptotic, requires consistency assumptions of the base estimators, and the recommended (used-in-experiments) implementation does not satisfy the finite-sample marginal guarantee. The ambitious 'Hypothesis B.8' about CQR under-coverage is left unproven and its central term ('non-trivial') is undefined.

Conditional coverage improvements are demonstrated primarily in simulations designed with specific extrapolation geometries (spheres, power-transformed means); no rigorous conditional-coverage metric (e.g., subgroup or nearest-neighbor conditional coverage) is reported on the real-world datasets, so the claim that CLEAR achieves 'improved conditional coverage' on real data is not directly evidenced.

Some headline comparisons are against ablations of the authors' own components (ALEATORIC/ALEATORIC-R vs. PCS) rather than established competing frameworks in the main text; comparisons to the closest prior method (UACQR) are relegated to a variant in the appendix.

The interval construction assumes additive separability of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty and a constant ratio λ across the input space; this structural choice is acknowledged but its limitations (e.g., heteroscedastic aleatoric with spatially varying epistemic-to-aleatoric ratios) are not empirically stress-tested.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: combining aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for regression intervals, with the two-parameter (γ1, λ) calibration giving a data-driven trade-off that fixed-ratio combinations (λ=1 or γ1=1) lack.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: 17 real-world datasets across 10 seeds, multiple estimator pairs (PCS/CQR, Deep Ensembles/SQR), three model variants (a/b/c) as ablations, plus a genuine case study (Ames Housing) demonstrating adaptive λ behavior under varying information regimes.

Honest and unusually thorough theoretical treatment: the finite-sample marginal coverage gap of the default (Dcal = Dval) implementation is explicitly acknowledged, and a conformalized variant with a formal guarantee (Lemma B.2) is provided; the asymptotic conditional coverage result (Lemma 2.1) is stated with assumptions discussed in detail.

Extensive supporting material: careful discussion of the quantile loss as a selection metric (properness, conditional calibration), limitations of conformal marginal guarantees under exchangeability violations, runtime analysis, and a very detailed related-work appendix.

Practical appeal: modularity (works with any aleatoric/epistemic estimator pair), negligible calibration overhead, and consistent gains over both component baselines (e.g., 9.4–34.5% quantile loss improvements and top performance on 15/17 datasets).
weaknesses: Novelty is modest relative to the claims: the core method is an additive combination of two uncertainty estimates with two scalar parameters, selected by grid search over λ with conformal calibration of γ1. This is a fairly incremental extension of CQR/UACQR [19] (which already tunes λ with γ1=1); the conceptual distance from UACQR is small, and the 'we are the first' claims in the contributions feel overstated.

The headline 'improved conditional coverage' claim rests on Lemma 2.1, which is essentially a consistency argument (consistent quantile estimators + ensemble variance vanishing asymptotically) — a known property of well-calibrated quantile methods — rather than a genuinely new finite-sample result. Conditional coverage evidence is limited to simulations with Gaussian features and well-specified ensembles.

The default configuration violates the conformal guarantee (Dcal = Dval, λ and γ1 both tuned on the same data), and the results favoring the default over the conformalized variant raise a question of how much of the reported gain comes from data reuse rather than the method itself. Overfitting λ over a 4000-point grid on small validation sets is acknowledged but only partially addressed.

The strongest baseline comparison (UACQR) appears only for variant (c) in the appendix, while the main paper compares mostly against the paper's own re-engineered components (PCS, ALEATORIC, ALEATORIC-R); a more prominent head-to-head with the closest published method is needed.

Heavy dependence on PCS-UQ [30], which appears to be concurrent/unpublished arXiv work, makes the primary experimental pipeline hard to fully assess and partially weakens the independent significance of the contribution.

Scope is limited to tabular regression; no experiments on images, text, or time series despite framing as a general UQ framework, and the empirical narrative in Section 4.2 contains redundant/repeated text and results normalized to CLEAR (baseline=1.0), which complicates absolute interpretation.
